Let me analyze these teaching examples carefully to identify systematic forecast errors and derive correction rules.

Looking at Example 1 (2025-03-11):
- History shows prices declining from ~79.75 down to ~69.01 over 18 days
- The model forecasts are also declining but seem to be lagging or not declining enough
- Looking at the comparison: model starts at 68.38 vs true 68.24 (close), but diverges
- The model appears to be too slow to follow price declines, especially in the middle section
- Around days 6-10: model is ~73-74 but true is ~71-72 (about 1-2 points too high)
- Around days 16-18: model is ~74 but true is ~68-69 (about 4-6 points too high!)

Looking at Example 2 (2024-06-19):
- History: prices declining from ~75.78 down to ~68.38 over 18 days
- Model forecasts: starts at 70.66 vs true 70.74 (close), but diverges
- Looking at the pattern - model seems to be consistently above true values in many places
- Days 6-10: model is 67.74-72.67 vs true 66.49-70.93 (model is often 1-3 points too high)
- Days 16-18: model is 71.02-71.72 vs true 68.52-69.35 (model is about 3-4 points too high)

Example 3 (2024-06-20) is essentially the same as Example 2 (just 1 day later), with the same errors.

Example 4 (2024-06-18):
- Similar pattern to Example 2
- Model forecasts are consistently slightly too high compared to true outcomes


- The divergence appears to be around 1-3 points in the early days, gradually increasing to 4-5 points in later sections

Example 5 (2024-05-24) reveals an interesting contrast:
- History shows prices rising from ~69.20 up to ~76.67 over 18 days

- Early sections show minimal divergence (~0.01-0.5 points), but later sections demonstrate more significant underperformance
